title: Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation

concept.text: The innovation is an integrated quantum computer that can perform a universal set of operations on encoded logical qubits, with errors per operation decreasing as the error-correcting code grows. A logical qubit distributes quantum information across multiple physical qubits. Increasing code distance increases the protection available against errors. The goal is to use that protection throughout a computation, so that larger and deeper circuits remain reliable when sufficient error-correction resources are added.

Preserving encoded information is one component; computing universally with it requires more. Fault-tolerant Clifford operations must work together with a suitable non-Clifford resource, for example the T gate, while error detection, decoding and feedback continue throughout the run. Memory protection, logical gates and resource preparation must function as one system. Increasing circuit depth does not itself lower logical error: increasing code distance must lower error per operation sufficiently to control the accumulated failure probability of the larger workload.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would make quantum computation an extendable experimental instrument: increasingly large universal circuits could be executed reliably by allocating more protection. Existing demonstrations already include encoded memories and distance-scalable logical Clifford circuits. The revolutionary step would be sustaining the integrated universal computation, including its non-Clifford operations and classical control, as the workload grows. The powered-flight analogy is useful as a description of that transition, but it should not imply that one finite experiment proves unlimited scalability or every assumption underlying fault-tolerance theory.

The direct consequence would be reliable composition of universal logical operations. Selected workloads could then produce results beyond credible classical simulation and still permit task-specific checks or independent experimental reproduction. Those properties require suitable workloads and verification protocols: universality and error correction alone do not guarantee useful quantum advantage or efficient verification of arbitrary outputs. Repeating a result can measure reproducibility without establishing that it is correct.

Synthesis across the supplied concepts: this platform could enable cryptographically relevant Shor execution, validated predictions of difficult quantum matter and other applications, but each would require its own execution and validation evidence. Practical impact would also depend on physical-qubit overhead, runtime, resource preparation and application development. Millions of logical qubits would describe one possible machine scale; that count is neither a separate computational principle nor a necessary completion threshold for this innovation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied demonstrations is integrated universal encoded computation with distance-dependent error suppression across the complete operation set. The Helios discussion specifically identifies below-threshold scaling of high-fidelity magic-state preparation, followed by a full Clifford-plus-T circuit with real-time decoding, as further work. Improving a memory or demonstrating protected Clifford circuits does not establish that the non-Clifford resources and their use will scale successfully within the same machine.

The engineering barriers interact. Gate errors must remain correctable during logical operations; leakage out of the computational states must be controlled; correlated bursts must not defeat the protection gained from larger codes. Decoders must process the error information fast enough, and feedback must arrive when subsequent operations require it. A system that decodes recorded data successfully after the experiment has demonstrated an important component, but has not yet demonstrated the full timing and control requirements of an operating universal computer.

Scaling also requires controlling total failure probability across increasing circuit width and depth, rather than reporting a low error rate for one isolated component. The Willow paper cites error rates below 10^-10 for many applications, illustrating the distance between its memory result and demanding workloads. That figure is application-dependent, not a universal requirement for every useful computation. The applications perspective likewise describes widely varying resource requirements, alongside further hardware, compilation and application-development work.

current_state.text: Google Quantum AI’s Willow study, published online on 9 December 2024 and appearing in Nature 638, 920–926 (2025), reports a 101-qubit distance-7 surface-code memory. Its logical error is 0.143% per correction cycle, with uncertainty of ±0.003 percentage points. The reported suppression factor is Λ = 2.14 ± 0.02 for each increase of two in code distance. This establishes below-threshold memory performance over the tested distances; the paper explicitly distinguishes the demonstrated memory from the additional challenges of logical computation.

The same study reports rare correlated bursts approximately once per hour in repetition-code experiments. These events matter for understanding long-running error correction, but their observation does not establish an identical error floor in a surface code. The supplied research also records an author correction dated 28 April 2026. Its contents were not revisited in the supplied material, so its effect on the reported findings remains unresolved.

Quantinuum’s Helios preprint, identified in the supplied research as dated 16 October 2026, reports color-code memories at distances 3, 5 and 7, with logical error rates as low as 5×10^-6. It also reports two-qubit logical Clifford randomized benchmarking at distances 3 and 5, including approximately 7×10^-5 error per logical two-qubit Clifford at distance 5. These results extend the demonstrated scope beyond memory to distance-scalable logical gate circuits. They remain preprint findings, and the tested Clifford sequences reach 209 gates.

Helios describes its error rates as approaching those required for megaquop-scale computation, roughly a million operations; it does not report an executed million-operation computation. All experimental decoding was performed offline, alongside separate streaming timing studies. The authors identify scalable magic-state preparation and an integrated Clifford-plus-T circuit with real-time decoding as next steps. The reported memory and Clifford results therefore do not establish the complete universal capability defined here.

The supplied research attributes a separate non-Clifford resource-preparation result to a Science publication dated 15 October 2026: a distance-3 cultivation experiment reportedly reduced error by a factor of 40, achieved state fidelity of at least 0.9999(1), and retained 8% of attempts. These details remain unverified in the supplied evidence review. The research records a failed full-text fetch, and the source index contains no captured abstract or full-text artifact for that citation. The claim is therefore retained as an attributed report, without treating its numbers, experimental scope or publication details as established here. The access limitation is not evidence that the result is false.

The Grand Challenge of Quantum Applications describes several platforms as operating below error-correction threshold and presents substantial remaining engineering and application-development work. Its statement that experimentalists believe current technology can scale to at least hundreds of logical qubits is an assessment, not a demonstrated machine size. Its resource estimates vary widely; some workloads are near or below a million Toffoli operations, so claims that applications uniformly require much longer jobs would overstate the evidence.

The perspective’s retained text contains a 4 December 2025 arXiv header and an August 24, 2026 body date. The research interpreted the latter as a conversion stamp and reported a 15 June 2026 journal publication from an APS listing, but the journal DOI page was inaccessible and the listing is not included in the supplied source index. Its precise publication chronology is therefore unresolved here. The retained HTML truncates during the references, although the review had the relevant application and verification discussion. Taken together, the supplied demonstrations do not establish integrated distance-scalable universal computation; they also do not establish whether another group had completed it worldwide by 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate an encoded universal gate set, such as Clifford plus T, across a family of increasing code distances. On comparable logical workloads, show that error per operation decreases with distance, with quantified uncertainty. Then demonstrate controlled total failure probability as circuit width and depth increase. Include non-Clifford resource preparation and consumption, decoding and timely feedback within the evaluated system. This proposal extends the integrated universal-circuit goal identified in the Helios discussion; it is not an established institutional standard.
completion_criteria.label: Universal encoded gates whose error per operation falls with code distance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed workload and verification test: include a computation whose relevant output is beyond credible classical simulation methods, and explain the evidence for that boundary. Circuit length alone does not establish classical hardness. Check the result using a task-appropriate classical test or an independent experiment where available. Use repeated runs to quantify uncertainty and reproducibility, while distinguishing agreement between runs from evidence of correctness.
completion_criteria.label: Computation beyond credible classical simulation with hardness evidence and checks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accounting and reproducibility test: report acceptance probability, discarded attempts, physical resources, resource-preparation costs, decoder latency and total runtime. Discarding most complete computation attempts should not satisfy this proposal. Heralded or repeat-until-success preparation of resources may be part of the architecture, provided its full cost and effect on throughput are included. Repeat the demonstration across separate runs and operating periods, and seek independent reproduction of the central scaling behavior.
completion_criteria.label: Report full resource costs and repeat scaling, seeking independent reproduction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: state the tested distances, logical-qubit counts, circuit families, depths, operating conditions and observed rare-event limits. Finite experiments can establish demonstrated breadth and scaling over those ranges, not literal universality across every possible circuit or indefinite operation. Neither millions of logical qubits nor one fixed numerical error threshold is required by this proposal; the demonstrated workload and its total failure budget should determine the necessary protection.
completion_criteria.label: State demonstrated ranges, rare-event limits, and workload total failure budget

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: QUA-02, Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm, is a particular application milestone that would require an adequate fault-tolerant machine plus successful execution at a cryptographically relevant scale. QUA-03, Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter, adds a different requirement: predictive results validated against physical evidence. Neither application follows merely from demonstrating the universal platform in QUA-01.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-04, A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature, concerns passive protection of stored information. It could contribute to an architecture but does not itself supply universal logical operations. QUA-05, Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons, specifies a particular physical route to universal computation. It overlaps QUA-01’s computational objective while adding distinct requirements for realizing and controlling the anyonic system; the entries retain separate identities.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-06, Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules, addresses reliable links between processors. Such links could support a modular implementation of QUA-01, while leaving universal operations within and across modules to be demonstrated. QUA-08, Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls, imposes a stronger resource-scaling objective. QUA-01 permits increasing error-correction resources as accuracy improves and does not require bounded overhead.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-07, A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems, is a mathematical complexity separation. Hardware demonstrations, even compelling ones beyond credible classical simulation, do not prove that separation. QUA-09, An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data, requires an application-level advantage that includes data handling and the complete workflow. Reliable universal hardware alone does not establish that speedup.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-10, Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator, adds manufacturing and operating-environment requirements to fault-tolerant computation. QUA-01 is independent of those particular requirements and could be demonstrated using another fabrication route or cryogenic architecture. The two milestones could overlap in one machine without becoming the same innovation.

change_log.change: Clarified that increasing code distance suppresses logical error per operation, while growing circuit width and depth increases the accumulated-error burden.
change_log.reason: The earlier wording could imply that error decreases simply because a computation becomes larger or deeper.

change_log.change: Defined the target as integrated universal computation with non-Clifford resources, decoding and feedback, while acknowledging demonstrated logical Clifford circuits.
change_log.reason: The original opening understated current gate demonstrations and did not fully distinguish component achievements from the integrated capability.

change_log.change: Preserved Willow’s numerical results, expressed its uncertainty in percentage points, and specified that Λ applies to distance increases of two.
change_log.reason: These details make the reported error and scaling quantities unambiguous.

change_log.reason: The observed events cannot be transferred unchanged between code experiments, and the correction’s contents were not supplied.

change_log.reason: No captured source artifact supports inspection, but missing evidence does not justify declaring the result false or removing the underlying concept.

change_log.reason: Those additional properties do not follow automatically from universal fault tolerance.

unresolved_issues: The Science citation has no captured artifact. Its identity, reported 15 October 2026 publication date, distance-3 scope, factor-of-40 error reduction, fidelity of at least 0.9999(1), and 8% acceptance remain unverified.
The contents and implications of the Willow author correction reported as published on 28 April 2026 remain unresolved.

The applications perspective’s precise publication chronology remains unresolved. The review’s conservative treatment is adopted because the conversion-stamp explanation and reported journal date cannot be settled from the supplied retained evidence.
Worldwide completion status as of 1 November 2026 is unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The completion criteria remain proposals. Workload selection, verification protocols, resource budgets and acceptable total failure probabilities require concrete experimental specification.
The Helios findings are preprint results; independent reproduction and integrated real-time universal operation are not established by the supplied material.

brief.title: Quantum computers that stay reliable as jobs grow
possible: Researchers could run longer, larger quantum calculations reliably by adding more error protection. Each logical qubit—a unit of quantum information spread across physical components—would become better protected, and errors would fall across the full range of computing operations.
why: This would give researchers an instrument for calculations beyond ordinary computers, including predictions about difficult quantum materials. Reliable operations could be combined into increasingly demanding experiments, with results checked against suitable tests or independent experiments.

sources.showed: Their Willow processors stored quantum information more reliably as protection increased. They also maintained error suppression while interpreting error signals during operation.
sources.quote: In this work, we realize surface codes operating below the threshold on two Willow processors.
sources.cited_for: Increasing protection can reduce errors in quantum memory, including with error processing during operation.
sources.not_established: Protected storage does not establish a complete set of computing operations that improve together as protection grows.

sources.showed: Their Helios preprint reports falling errors as protection increased for memory and Clifford gates, a limited family of computing operations. Tested sequences reached 209 gates.
sources.quote:
we demonstrate below threshold scaling of error rates for Clifford two-qubit
randomized benchmarking circuits
sources.cited_for: Error suppression with growing protection extends beyond storage to a limited family of computing operations.
sources.not_established: The preprint does not demonstrate the full operation set with error processing and feedback during computation.

sources.who: The authors of the resource-preparation study
sources.showed: This is an experimental study of preparing special quantum states needed for operations beyond the Clifford family.
sources.cited_for: Preparing resources for the remaining computing operations is a separate experimental challenge.
sources.not_established: Resource preparation alone does not establish reliable universal computation as protection grows.

sources.who: Ryan Babbush and colleagues, Google Quantum AI
sources.showed: Their perspective describes the work needed to turn quantum algorithms into useful applications, including finding hard problems, checking answers and accounting for resources.
sources.cited_for: Useful applications require suitable problems and ways to assess the quality of their answers.
sources.not_established: The perspective does not demonstrate an application running on an integrated, protected quantum computer.

sources.showed: An earlier version of the same work.

shown: Google Quantum AI demonstrated quantum memory that improved with added protection. Quantinuum went further into computing: its Helios preprint reports the same trend for protected Clifford gate sequences. Together, these results establish important components of the proposed machine.
missing: A complete operation set must show falling errors as protection grows, including preparation and use of the special quantum states it needs.
Error interpretation and timely feedback must work throughout the complete computation, rather than only after it finishes.
Larger and longer calculations must keep their overall chance of failure under control.

milestones.label: All computing operations improve with added protection
milestones.explanation: A full operation set, including resource preparation, error processing and timely feedback, would have to improve with added protection as calculations grow. This would establish reliable computing beyond memory and limited gates.

milestones.label: A checked result beyond credible ordinary computer simulation
milestones.explanation: A computation would have to exceed credible ordinary simulation methods, with evidence of difficulty, suitable checks and measured reproducibility. This would connect reliable operation to a result ordinary computers cannot match.

milestones.label: Full costs and repeated scaling results
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to count discarded attempts, hardware, preparation, control delays and runtime, repeat across operating periods and seek independent reproduction. This would establish practical costs without discarding most whole runs.

milestones.label: Measured operating ranges and failure limits
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to state protection levels, calculation sizes, operating conditions, rare errors and overall failure budgets. This would define the demonstrated range without treating finite tests as proof of unlimited operation.

uncertain: Rare errors affecting many components at once may limit how much extra protection helps during long computations.
Helios remains a preprint result, and independent reproduction of its scaling behavior remains open.
The proposed milestones still need concrete workloads, checking methods, resource budgets and acceptable overall failure probabilities.

page.title: Below-threshold universal quantum computation
page.definition: A quantum computer executes encoded operations sufficient to approximate arbitrary quantum circuits, with lower error per logical operation as code distance increases. One such universal set combines Clifford gates with a non-Clifford gate called T. A logical qubit stores information across physical qubits. Code distance is the fewest physical qubits on which an error can act undetected while changing the encoded information. A decoder interprets error-check measurements so later operations can use the corrected outcomes.

goal.need: Chemists tracing a reaction mechanism may need energies for thousands of candidate steps. Density functional calculations can locate plausible structures yet give uncertain energy differences. More accurate energies could help distinguish competing pathways, including those for nitrogen fixation. At a fixed error rate per gate, errors accumulate as a quantum calculation grows. Correcting them during execution would make longer calculations possible. Some proposed applications also need hundreds to thousands of logical qubits operating through billions of gates.

figures.caption: Error scales contrasted in the Willow study
rows: Error rate required for many applications
figures.note: Physical infidelity is calculated as one minus the cited 99.9% fidelity. These quantities are not an identical operational error metric; application requirements depend on the workload.

statements.quote: The ultimate goal is to demonstrate a pathway to achieving the low errors needed for using quantum computers in meaningful applications.
Error-corrected logical qubits are needed to achieve this goal.
statements.context: The preceding sentence identifies the goal as executing long algorithms with end-to-end error rates below those physical qubits can support directly.

statements.body: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
statements.quote: possible future pathways toward a universal, fault-tolerant quantum computer
statements.context: Chapter 7 of Quantum Computing: Progress and Prospects identifies milestones on those pathways, including error-corrected qubits with better error rates than physical qubits.

completion.title: Universal logical circuits show below-threshold scaling with real-time decoding.
completion.criterion: Execute comparable encoded circuits containing a universal set of operations at increasing code distances, with repeated error checks, real-time decoding and any feedback the circuit requires. The logical error per operation for the full circuit, including its non-Clifford operations, must decrease. For distances d and d+2 this means ε_d/ε_(d+2) > 1. In the proposed color-code test, run Clifford-plus-T circuits with preparation and consumption of the magic states used to teleport T gates.
completion.set_by: The below-threshold distance-scaling convention. The Quantinuum Helios team specifies a Clifford-plus-T color-code experiment in its Discussion.
completion.threshold_quote: below threshold behavior on a full Clifford plus T circuit encoded in color code using real-time decoding of the syndromes.
completion.basis: The proposed experiment extends a distance comparison from memory and Clifford gates to a full universal circuit. An algorithm at one distance shows that its components can operate together. Establishing scaling requires the distance comparison on the integrated computation. The proposal specifies neither a circuit length nor a statistical significance cutoff.

milestones.title: A logical memory outlasts its best constituent physical qubit.
milestones.criterion: Compare the error-corrected logical memory with its best constituent physical qubit on the same storage task. The logical memory lifetime must exceed that physical-qubit lifetime.
milestones.set_by: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Quantum Computing: Progress and Prospects, section 7.3.4, milestone G2b; the memory comparison is operationalized in the Willow study.
milestones.threshold_quote: yielding one or more logical qubits of better error rates than possible with physical qubits

milestones.title: Logical memory errors decrease with code distance, with suppression factor Λ > 1.
milestones.criterion: Measure the logical memory error probability per correction cycle, ε_d, for the same storage task at increasing code distances d. For distances d and d+2, the suppression factor Λ = ε_d/ε_(d+2) must exceed 1.
milestones.set_by: The below-threshold quantum error-correction convention, expressed quantitatively in the Willow study, equation 1 and the following definition of Λ.
milestones.threshold_quote: representing the reduction in logical error rate when increasing the code distance by two

milestones.title: Error per logical two-qubit Clifford decreases with code distance.
milestones.criterion: Run two-qubit Clifford randomized benchmarking at increasing code distances. Sample sequences of logical Clifford gates at several lengths, apply the inverse of each sequence, and estimate error per logical two-qubit Clifford from the decay of the return probability. For distances d and d+2, the ratio of the lower-distance error to the higher-distance error must exceed 1.
milestones.set_by: The below-threshold convention applied to logical two-qubit Clifford randomized benchmarking by the Quantinuum Helios team; its published implementation uses color codes.
milestones.threshold_quote: below threshold scaling of error rates for Clifford two-qubit randomized benchmarking circuits

milestones.title: Logical non-Clifford gates use real-time decoding and measurement-conditioned feedback.
milestones.criterion: Execute a logical non-Clifford operation with repeated error checks. Decode the relevant measurements during execution and use the decoded outcome to select the correction or subsequent gate before the step that depends on it.
milestones.set_by: Microsoft Quantum and Qolab, Scalable logical qubits, capability items 4 and 5: universal operations and measurement-conditioned control under repeated error correction.
milestones.threshold_quote: allow program execution to branch on measurement outcomes, requiring low-latency real-time decoding, feedforward

milestones.title: Logical non-Clifford errors decrease as code distance grows, with suppression factor Λ > 1.
milestones.criterion: The non-Clifford operation or its prepared resource has decreasing logical error as code distance grows. Superconducting: the cultivation preprint version of 15 December 2025 reports a d = 3 fidelity lower bound of 0.9999(1), retaining 8% of attempts, and grafting into d = 5; it does not test this scaling. Trapped ions: Helios identifies this as remaining work. Neutral atoms: the 19 December 2024 preprint tests 5-to-1 distillation at d = 3 and 5, with 1,152,262 and 259,261 factory runs; it reports that the data-code gates are not yet below their circuit threshold.
milestones.set_by: The below-threshold convention and Microsoft/Qolab reliability criterion; Quantinuum explicitly identifies the remaining resource-preparation test for color codes in the Helios Discussion.

milestones.title: An encoded qubit is protected against a specified class of physical errors.
milestones.criterion: Encode a qubit across physical qubits, expose it to an error the code is designed to correct, and demonstrate recovery of the encoded information. A three-qubit code correcting a single phase flip is one implementation.
milestones.set_by: Quantum Information Science and Technology Experts Panel, Quantum Computation Roadmap version 2.0, metric 4.6.

milestones.title: A simple algorithm runs fault tolerantly on three to ten logical qubits.
milestones.criterion: Execute a simple quantum algorithm on three to ten logical qubits using fault-tolerant logical operations. A demonstration at one code distance suffices for this stage.
milestones.set_by: Quantum Information Science and Technology Experts Panel, Quantum Computation Roadmap version 2.0, section 7, metric 7.5.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate fault-tolerant implementation of simple quantum algorithms with logical qubits.

milestones.title: The error in preparing an encoded magic state decreases with code distance.
milestones.criterion: Prepare the same target magic state at increasing code distances and compare the output-state infidelity, one minus its fidelity to the target. Infidelity must decrease with preparation distance. For a protocol that discards attempts, compare the preparation errors under a stated acceptance rule and report the fraction accepted at each distance.
milestones.set_by: The Quantinuum Helios team’s proposed test of below-threshold magic-state preparation in color codes.
milestones.threshold_quote: below threshold scaling of high-fidelity color code magic state preparation

milestones.title: The error per executed logical non-Clifford gate decreases with code distance.
milestones.criterion: Implement the same logical non-Clifford gate at increasing code distances and compare its error acting on the encoded data. Include the operations that apply the gate, including consumption of a prepared state when the implementation uses one. For distances d and d+2, the ratio of the gate error at d to that at d+2 must exceed 1.
milestones.set_by: The logical-error distance-scaling convention applied to Microsoft Quantum and Qolab’s requirement for fault-tolerant non-Clifford operations.
milestones.threshold_quote: increasing code distance (and corresponding resources) predictably reduces logical error rate

not_found: No platform-independent acceptance standard specifying circuit length, statistical significance or permissible postselection for the integrated universal-circuit test was located.
The Science full text for DOI 10.1126/science.aee7961 could not be opened; the accessible cultivation preprint was read.
Total shot counts underlying the cultivation fidelity lower bound were not located in the accessible text.
No experimental report was found showing lower error at increasing code distances for a full logical Clifford-plus-T circuit with real-time decoding.

results.finding: Distance-15 repetition-code recovery, 10⁶ repetitions per experiment: halving the detection probability reduced logical error 250-fold.
results.detail: The authors subsampled the distance-15 code from distance-29 data. Recovery was assessed from the decoded logical readout.
results.quote: For example, reducing the detection probability by a factor of 2 manifests in reduction by a factor of 250 in logical error at distance 15

results.finding: One 101-qubit distance-7 surface-code memory outlasted its best constituent physical qubit by a factor of 2.4 ± 0.3.
results.quote: The distance-7 logical qubit lifetime is 291 ± 6 μs, exceeding the lifetimes of all the constituent physical qubits (median, 85 ± 7 μs; best, 119 ± 13 μs) by a factor of 2.4 ± 0.3.

results.finding: Willow surface-code memory at distances 3, 5 and 7, with 10⁵ repetitions per data point, achieved Λ = 2.14 ± 0.02.
results.detail: The main fit used logical X and Z storage data through 250 cycles. Repetition-code data also showed suppression, with Λ = 8.4 ± 0.1 over distances 5–11.
results.quote:
The logical error rate of our larger quantum memory is suppressed by a factor of
Λ

definition = "A quantum computer executes encoded operations sufficient to approximate arbitrary quantum circuits, with lower error per logical operation as code distance increases. One such universal set combines Clifford gates with a non-Clifford gate called T. A logical qubit stores information across physical qubits. Code distance is the fewest physical qubits on which an error can act undetected while changing the encoded information. A decoder interprets error-check measurements so later operations can use the corrected outcomes.". Reason: The definition uses “weight” without explaining what it counts and leaves the role of a non-Clifford gate implicit.

goal.need = "Chemists tracing a reaction mechanism may need energies for thousands of candidate steps. Density functional calculations can locate plausible structures yet give uncertain energy differences. More accurate energies could help distinguish competing pathways, including those for nitrogen fixation. At a fixed error rate per gate, errors accumulate as a quantum calculation grows. Correcting them during execution would make longer calculations possible. Some proposed applications also need hundreds to thousands of logical qubits operating through billions of gates.". Reason: The current text describes a study and a gate set without identifying a calculation people need, its scale or the conditions for using it.

add statement by National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2019: "possible future pathways toward a universal, fault-tolerant quantum computer". Reason: The National Academies roadmap gives the entry an independent committee statement of the goal and connects it to the existing memory milestone.

edit completion: criterion = "Execute comparable encoded circuits containing a universal set of operations at increasing code distances, with repeated error checks, real-time decoding and any feedback the circuit requires. The logical error per operation for the full circuit, including its non-Clifford operations, must decrease. For distances d and d+2 this means \u03b5_d/\u03b5_(d+2) > 1. In the proposed color-code test, run Clifford-plus-T circuits with preparation and consumption of the magic states used to teleport T gates."; set_by = "The below-threshold distance-scaling convention. The Quantinuum Helios team specifies a Clifford-plus-T color-code experiment in its Discussion."; threshold_quote = "below threshold behavior on a full Clifford plus T circuit encoded in color code using real-time decoding of the syndromes."; threshold_ref = 2; basis = "The proposed experiment extends a distance comparison from memory and Clifford gates to a full universal circuit. An algorithm at one distance shows that its components can operate together. Establishing scaling requires the distance comparison on the integrated computation. The proposal specifies neither a circuit length nor a statistical significance cutoff."; refs = [2, 1, 4, 18]. Reason: The existing criterion makes magic-state preparation mandatory for every implementation although the Helios proposal assumes a particular way of implementing T gates.
add case "Silicon spin qubits". Reason: The French academy’s fault-tolerant computing roadmap treats spins in silicon as a distinct hardware platform.
add case "Photonic qubits". Reason: The same roadmap tracks photonic implementations separately, including fault-tolerant computation by measurements on entangled photons.
